newsitem.title: UK: Favourite Swift wins Britain's top literary prize.
newsitem.headline: Favourite Swift wins Britain's top literary prize.

text.p: Graham Swift on Tuesday won Britain's top literary prize with "Last Orders," a quirky tale of four friends of a London butcher scattering his ashes at sea.
Swift, whose novels have been translated into 20 languages, was the hottest favourite in the 28-year history of the prize.
Bookmakers had made the 47-year-old Londoner 4-7 favourite to land the 20,000 pound ($32,140) prize that will catapult him into the bestseller lists.
"I am absolutely all over the place. I am all of a wobble," he confessed after his victory.
"I don't think the Booker Prize, or any other literary prize, makes writers write. But prizes, particularly the Booker, are a tremendous boost to the reading of fiction," he said.
It was second time lucky for the English teacher who had been shortlisted for the prestigious prize once before in 1983 for "Waterland."
"I've certainly had my years of struggle," he said before pocketing the cheque that will transform his literary career.
"When I started out I had a lot of financial problems, but since Waterland I've managed to get by on my writing."
Carmen Callil, chairman of the judges, said: "Choosing the winner was torture but we finally settled on a wonderful book that will give great pleasure to thousands of people."
She attacked critics who denigrated the English novel, complaining: "A clique of critics have hovered in the shade of American fiction admiring their pistol-packing approach.
"It means that great English writers have been overlooked. They are in a no-win situation. There has been this obsessive denigration going on."

Beryl Bainbrige was in philosophical form after being on the Booker shortlist for the fourth time with "Every Man for Himself," an evocative recreation of the doomed maiden voyage of the Titanic. "It's all the luck of the draw," she said.
The judges read 150 books by writers from 50 Commonwealth countries and Ireland before picking their shortlist of six.
The six shortlisted authors, used to their lonely profession, confessed to being startled by the glare of publicity. But they felt it was worthwhile if their books reached a wider audience.

Northern Irish poet Seamus Deane, nominated for his first novel "Reading in the Dark," said: "It does feel a bit like a feeding frenzy and is a bit of a shock when you lead such a solitary existence."
Canadian writer Margaret Atwood, shortlisted for "Alias Grace," said of the prize: "It actively does encourage more reading but is hard on the authors, especially the younger ones.
"There is nothing you can do to win it. It's not like a horse race or the Olympics. Not having sex the night before won't help."
The other runners-up were Indian-born Rohinton Mistry, picked for "A Fine Balance," and Shena Mackay, chosen for "The Orchard on Fire."
